chapter_title: The Magic Brush of Dreams (Mystery and Magic)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 7 periods = 315 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 5h 15min

periods.activity_title: Entering the World of Gopi and Her Magic Brush

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read — pre-reading discussion (p.122): paired talk on magic objects and acts of kindness.
Let us discuss (p.127): arrange poem events in order of occurrence.

time_bands.activity: Open with the paired pre-reading discussion from “Let us read” (p.122): students share a magical object they’d like to own and what they would paint with a magic brush. Take brief whole-class responses to warm up the imagination.

Read the poem aloud together, teacher leading with students following in their textbooks (p.122–126). Pause at the stanza beginning “He slips the brush into her hand” to check understanding of the man’s condition, and again at the imprisonment stanza so students can anticipate what Gopi will do.

Work on “Let us discuss” (p.127): students individually sequence the ten events of the poem in their notebooks, then compare with a partner. Confirm the correct order as a class, emphasising how Gopi’s choices build the plot.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading talk activates personal connection to the poem’s central idea before the text is encountered. A common difficulty is that students read the poem’s stanzas as unconnected images rather than a continuous story—the sequencing task directly addresses this by asking them to track narrative causality. Students who finish sequencing early may annotate the events with a single emotion word for each stage of the story.
materials: Class textbook, “The Magic Brush of Dreams” (p.122–130)

periods.activity_title: Tone, Imagery, and Symbol in the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.127): fill in tone shifts — playful, tense, triumphant.
Let us think and reflect (p.128): give examples of imagery and explain effect of repetition.
Let us think and reflect (p.128): match phrases to their symbolic meanings.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.128): identify rhyme scheme and poetry genre — self-study.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the idea of tone by re-reading three short extracts: the opening sand-drawing stanza, the imprisonment stanza, and the final celebration stanza. Students fill in the tone-shift blanks from “Let us think and reflect” (p.127) individually, then discuss choices with a partner.

Guide students to locate vivid sensory details in the poem — the bowl of khichdi, the winding road, the mighty river — as examples of imagery from “Let us think and reflect” (p.128). Then focus on the line “On you, and you and you!”: students discuss in pairs what the repetition adds to the threat before sharing with the class.

Students complete the matching task (p.128) pairing the magic paintbrush, the grand fortress, and the river and beast with their symbolic meanings. Review as a class with brief justification for each match, asking students to point to lines in the poem that support their choices.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem as a continuous story, students are now asked to analyse its craft. A common difficulty at this stage is confusing the surface meaning of an image with its symbolic weight—prompt students to ask “what does this object stand for beyond itself?” when they tackle the matching task. The homework item on rhyme scheme and genre is light identification work that students can confirm by scanning the poem independently.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading: Extracts, Character, and Moral Judgement

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.129): extract 1 — significance of man giving brush to Gopi.
Let us think and reflect (p.129–30): extract 2 — Zamindar’s demand and character.
Let us think and reflect (p.130): discuss Gopi’s refusal and the poem’s moral.

time_bands.activity: Students re-read Extract 1 (p.129) silently, then answer the two short-response questions on the man’s secrecy and the significance of slipping the brush to Gopi. Pairs compare answers before a brief whole-class discussion on what the man’s condition reveals about the purpose of the brush.

Move to Extract 2 (p.129–30): teacher reads aloud the stanzas on news spreading and the Zamindar’s demand. Students answer the questions on why the poem calls Gopi’s creations ‘magic gains’ and what the Zamindar’s demand reveals about his character, writing responses in their notebooks.

Open discussion from “Let us think and reflect” (p.130): Was Gopi right to refuse the Zamindar? Students first think individually, then share in a whole-class exchange. Draw out the moral contrast between Gopi’s service to the poor and the Zamindar’s greed, and what the ending celebrates.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored tone and symbolism, students now read closely for character motivation and moral judgement—the poem’s two contrasting figures (Gopi and the Zamindar) are the axis around which all critical questions turn. Watch for students who evaluate Gopi’s choice as simply ‘brave’ without connecting it to the condition the man set—push them to link the man’s instruction (“Paint not for the wealthy ones”) to Gopi’s refusal. Tasks on comparing Gopi’s and the Zamindar’s use of the brush and justifying the title are available in the textbook (p.130) for students who wish to explore further independently.

periods.activity_title: Listening for Detail and Speaking with Intonation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.132): match five speakers’ magical wishes to seven statements.
Let us speak (p.131): read imperative lines from the poem with falling intonation.
Let us speak (p.131): make formal and informal requests in pairs.

time_bands.activity: Distribute or display the seven statements from “Let us listen” (p.132). Ask students to read them quickly and predict which magical powers are most likely to appear before the transcript is read.

Teacher reads the five-speaker transcript aloud at a natural pace (p.152) while students listen and match each statement to the correct speaker in their notebooks. Read once through, then a second time pausing between speakers so students can confirm or revise their matches.

Introduce falling intonation from “Let us speak” (p.131): teacher models the four imperative lines from the poem (“Come here!”, “Seize this magic brush…”, “Paint my fortress tall!”, “Go and fetch some rice”) with exaggerated falling tone, then students practise in chorus and then individually.

Paired request practice from “Let us speak” (p.131): assign three pairs a formal situation and three pairs an informal situation. Each pair drafts one request using the suggested phrases, then performs it for an adjacent pair for peer feedback on tone and register.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening task requires students to distinguish between closely related magical powers (predicting the future versus making wise business decisions); encourage them to focus on the specific benefit each speaker describes rather than the broad category of the power. For the intonation practice, students who speak hesitantly in class benefit from the choral step before individual performance—keep the atmosphere playful by framing it as delivering the Zamindar’s commands.

periods.activity_title: The Many Meanings of ‘Draw’ and the Grammar of Feeling: Interjections

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.130): match six sentences using ‘draw’ to their correct contextual meanings.
Let us learn (p.132): match interjections to emotions, then use five in original sentences.

time_bands.activity: Write the word ‘draw’ on the board and elicit its meanings from students using quick contextual prompts (“Gopi draws in the sand”; “the news draws the Zamindar’s attention”). Students then complete the matching task from “Let us learn” (p.130), pairing each of the six sentences with the correct meaning from the column.

Review the ‘draw’ matches as a class, asking students to read the sentence aloud and state the meaning before confirming. Highlight that context—what follows or precedes the verb—is the key to choosing the right meaning.

Introduce interjections using the matching task from “Let us learn” (p.132): students first match each interjection to its emotion independently, then write five original sentences using five of the seven expressions. Select three or four students to share a sentence; the class identifies the emotion conveyed.

periods.teacher_notes: The polysemy of ‘draw’ is the central challenge here—students tend to default to its most familiar meaning (to sketch or depict) and need to be pushed to read the surrounding clause for semantic clues. The interjection task moves from recognition to production: ensure that the sentences students write place the interjection at the moment of reaction rather than as a decorative opener, as the poem’s own exclamatory lines (“No beans, no rice, no mangoes!”) model. The crossword activity is available in the textbook (p.131) for students who wish to extend their vocabulary independently.

periods.activity_title: Writing an Imaginative Essay: Planning, Drafting, and Revising

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.133): plan, draft, and revise an imaginative essay on a chosen prompt.

time_bands.activity: Read the sample imaginative essay (‘My Life as EcoFlash’) aloud with the class, then go through the checklist of what an imaginative essay includes (p.133). Discuss the two prompt options briefly so students understand the scope before they choose.

Students plan their essay individually: a brief note on setting, key events (3–4 points), and what they learned or valued from the experience. Teacher circulates to help students who struggle to expand their initial idea.

Students write their draft essay in their notebooks, following the checklist as a guide. Encourage vivid, sensory detail in the style of the poem’s earthy imagery (khichdi, a winding road, a strong horse).

Paired peer response: partners exchange drafts and tick each item on the checklist, noting one specific strength and one place where a detail could be more vivid. Students make one revision based on the feedback before the exchange ends.

periods.teacher_notes: The imaginative essay calls for the same quality of sensory, inventive language the poem models, so referring students back to the poem’s concrete images as a stylistic touchstone is useful when they plan. The most common difficulty is that students list events without giving emotional or evaluative weight to them—prompt them to ask “what did this experience feel like, and what did it teach you?” at the planning stage. Planning, drafting, peer response, and a revision cycle are all contained within this sitting so the essay is complete by the end.
materials: Class textbook (p.133–134, sample essay and checklist)

periods.activity_title: Words That Play Tricks: Riddles and a Magical Creation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.136): solve four riddles about seemingly unreal things.
Let us explore (p.136): design a magical object with a drawing and description of its special quality.

time_bands.activity: Share a brief note on P. C. Sorcar Sr. from “Let us explore” (p.136) to connect the poem’s theme of magic with real-world illusion and performance. Invite students to name any magicians or magical performances they know.

Students attempt the four riddles from “Let us explore” (p.136) individually in their notebooks, then compare answers with a partner. Discuss as a class: what makes these riddles feel ‘magical’—the gap between the description and the answer—linking back to the poem’s theme that ordinary things can be seen with extraordinary eyes.

Students design their magical object from “Let us explore” (p.136): they draw the object, label its parts, and write a short description of its special quality on the same sheet. Encourage objects that serve a community need, echoing Gopi’s condition to help the poor.
Quick gallery share: students hold up or briefly describe their magical object to the class in one sentence. Celebrate the variety of objects and the reasoning behind each special quality.

periods.teacher_notes: The riddle activity extends the poem’s playful sense of the ordinary made extraordinary—sound, footsteps, a map, a candle are all ‘magical’ because they defy literal description. When students design their magical object, the most compelling pieces will be those where the object’s special quality solves a real problem (as Gopi’s painted gifts do), so redirect students who choose purely fantastical powers toward a community use. The display-board instruction in the textbook is optional and can be carried out if the classroom has a display space.
materials: Plain drawing paper or sketchbook pages

items.source_context: Gopi’s plot arc: sand-drawing, magic brush gift, helping villagers, imprisonment, escape, celebration.
items.item_stem:
Read the events from “The Magic Brush of Dreams” listed below. Identify which event happens FIRST in the poem.
(A) The Zamindar throws Gopi into prison.
(B) Gopi paints a bowl of khichdi that becomes real.
(C) A man on a stone gives Gopi the magic brush with a condition.
(D) Gopi paints a winding road and a horse to escape the prison.

options.label: A
options.text: A man on a stone gives Gopi the magic brush with a condition.

options.label: B
options.text: Gopi paints a bowl of khichdi that becomes real.

options.label: C
options.text: Gopi paints a winding road and a horse to escape the prison.

options.label: D
options.text: The Zamindar throws Gopi into prison.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have focused on the poem’s most dramatic event rather than its opening sequence.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student recalls a key early event but confuses it with the very first narrative turning point.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student is working backwards from the poem’s climax rather than its beginning.

items.source_lo: Student identifies sequence and narrative structure using a narrative poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Gopi’s plot arc: sand-drawing, magic brush gift, helping villagers, imprisonment, escape, celebration.
items.item_stem: In the poem, Gopi’s first act with the magic brush is to paint a bowl of khichdi for her family. Explain how this single act drives the rest of the poem’s plot forward. Use at least two events from the poem to support your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The bowl of khichdi becomes real and the villagers stream in to see it, spreading the news of Gopi’s magic brush far and wide. This fame reaches the Zamindar, who then demands Gopi paint treasures for him, setting off the conflict that leads to her imprisonment and escape.

items.source_context: Tone arc (playful to tense to triumphant), sensory imagery, magic brush and fortress as symbols.
items.item_stem:
Fill in the blanks using the words in the box to complete the statement about tone in the poem.
[ tense and suspenseful / playful and innocent / triumphant and celebratory ]

When Gopi sits beneath the banyan tree drawing pictures in the sand, the tone is 1. ________________. As the Zamindar imprisons Gopi and demands she paint riches for him, the tone becomes 2. ________________. At the poem’s close, when Gopi paints a feast and a band plays in the courtyard, the tone shifts to 3. ________________.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. playful and innocent  2. tense and suspenseful  3. triumphant and celebratory

items.source_context: Tone arc (playful to tense to triumphant), sensory imagery, magic brush and fortress as symbols.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the magic brush and the grand fortress represent very different values. Read the lines beginning “I order you to paint for me” and explain what the Zamindar’s fortress symbolises. Then contrast this with what the magic brush symbolises for Gopi and the villagers. Use evidence from the poem in your response.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The Zamindar’s fortress symbolises greed and the desire for power and wealth, as he wants it to help him “rule this land”. In contrast, the magic brush symbolises the transformative power of art and imagination used in service of justice, since Gopi uses it to provide food, warmth, and tools to the poor.

items.source_lo: Student evaluates character motivation and moral judgement using a narrative poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Man’s condition to Gopi, Zamindar’s greed, Gopi’s refusal, moral contrast between service and oppression.
items.item_stem:
Which of the following statements best explains why the man who gave Gopi the brush told her to keep it secret from the village?
(A) He feared the villagers would take the brush away from Gopi.
(B) He wanted Gopi to use the brush before anyone could stop her.
(C) He knew that the power of the brush would attract greedy people if it became known.
(D) He planned to return and take the brush back once Gopi had used it.

options.label: A
options.text: He feared the villagers would take the brush away from Gopi.

options.label: B
options.text: He knew that the power of the brush would attract greedy people if it became known.

options.label: C
options.text: He planned to return and take the brush back once Gopi had used it.

options.label: D
options.text: He wanted Gopi to use the brush before anyone could stop her.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student misidentifies the threat as coming from the villagers rather than from those in power.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student focuses on urgency but misses the poem’s established reason that secrecy protects the brush from the powerful.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student introduces a motive not supported anywhere in the poem.

items.source_lo: Student evaluates character motivation and moral judgement using a narrative poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Man’s condition to Gopi, Zamindar’s greed, Gopi’s refusal, moral contrast between service and oppression.
items.item_stem: Gopi chooses to paint a river and threaten the Zamindar with a beast rather than comply with his demands. What does this choice reveal about her character, and do you think her decision to use threat rather than simply flee was the right one? Give reasons for your view.

expected_elements: Identifies Gopi as courageous and principled, not merely self-protective.
Notes that the river and beast protect the villagers, not just Gopi herself.
Evaluates the choice: threat secures a permanent retreat, mere flight would not.
Supports view with specific details from the poem.

items.item_stem:
Read the statements below. Based on the spoken transcript, select which statement correctly describes Speaker (iii).
(A) Speaker (iii) wants a power that would help crops receive the right amount of rain.
(B) Speaker (iii) wants the ability to travel quickly without using any transport.
(C) Speaker (iii) wants to remember information instantly to make exams easier.
(D) Speaker (iii) wants the power to heal family members and reduce their physical pain.

options.label: A
options.text: Speaker (iii) wants a power that would help crops receive the right amount of rain.

options.label: B
options.text: Speaker (iii) wants the ability to travel quickly without using any transport.

options.label: C
options.text: Speaker (iii) wants the power to heal family members and reduce their physical pain.

options.label: D
options.text: Speaker (iii) wants to remember information instantly to make exams easier.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses Speaker (iii) with Speaker (v), who specifically mentions crops and rain.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student confuses Speaker (iii) with Speaker (ii), who mentions exams and cricket.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses Speaker (iii) with Speaker (iv), who discusses healing aches and family health.

items.source_lo: Student listens for specific detail and matches information to speakers using an oral transcript as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five speakers each describe one desired magical power: predict future, instant learning, flying, healing, weather control.
items.item_stem: Two of the five speakers wish for powers that would directly benefit other people, not just themselves. Identify those two speakers and explain, using details from what each says, how their chosen power would help others.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Speaker (i) wishes to predict the future and explicitly says they would use it to help others make wise financial decisions. Speaker (iv) wishes for the power of healing and says they would heal not just their own aches but also their family members to keep them healthy and happy.

items.item_stem: Read aloud the following imperative line from the poem with the correct falling intonation: “Go and fetch some rice.” Then say a second imperative sentence of your own in the same falling tone, as if you are the Zamindar giving an order to his men.

expected_elements: Clear falling tone on the stressed word at the end of the line.
Second sentence is an imperative in form and appropriate to context.
Confident, audible delivery without rising or questioning inflection.
Sentence invented by student, not a repetition of the prompt line.

items.source_lo: Student uses appropriate intonation and register in oral communication using guided speaking tasks as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Falling intonation in imperatives from the poem; formal and informal request phrases.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are a student who wants to persuade your class teacher to organise a drama performance based on “The Magic Brush of Dreams.” Make a formal spoken request to your teacher, giving at least one reason why the performance would benefit the class. Your request should take about one minute.

expected_elements: Opens with a formal address (e.g., “Excuse me, Ma’am / Sir”).
States the request clearly and politely without commanding tone.
Gives a relevant reason linked to the poem or learning benefit.
Maintains formal register throughout (no casual language or slang).

items.source_lo: Student plans, drafts, and revises an imaginative essay using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Imaginative essay: inanimate object or magical encounter prompt; checklist for essay structure and sensory detail.
items.item_stem: Write a short imaginative essay (about 150 words) with the following prompt as your guide: Imagine you are a twig — like the one Gopi used to draw pictures in the sand — that is picked up by a child in a different part of the world. Describe what the child draws with you, what you see and feel, and what happens to you at the end of the day. Use sensory details and write in the first person.

expected_elements: Writes in first person from the twig’s perspective consistently.
Includes at least two sensory details (touch, sight, sound, or smell).
Describes a specific drawing the child makes and gives it meaning.
Has a clear ending — what happens to the twig by day’s close.

items.source_lo: Student plans, drafts, and revises an imaginative essay using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Imaginative essay: inanimate object or magical encounter prompt; checklist for essay structure and sensory detail.
items.item_stem: In “The Magic Brush of Dreams,” Gopi uses her magical ability to serve the community rather than herself. Write an imaginative essay (about 200 words) in which you discover a magical power of your own. Explain: (a) what the power is, (b) how you discovered it, (c) one difficult choice you faced in using it, and (d) what you learned from that experience. Your essay should have a clear beginning, middle, and end, and should reflect your own point of view.

expected_elements: Describes a specific magical power with a clear discovery moment.
Presents a genuine moral or practical dilemma in using the power.
Reflects on what the experience taught them; goes beyond a plot summary.
Essay has a recognisable structure: opening, development, resolution.

items.source_context: Verb ‘draw’ in six distinct contextual meanings drawn from varied sentence types.
items.item_stem: The verb “draw” can mean “got a reaction” in one of its uses. Write two original sentences about Gopi or the events in the poem “The Magic Brush of Dreams” using the verb “draw”: one sentence where it means “got a reaction” and one where it means “attract.” Underline the word “draw” (or its past form) in each sentence.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any two grammatically correct sentences grounded in the poem. Example 1 (got a reaction): “Gopi’s painted bowl of khichdi drew gasps of amazement from the villagers.” Example 2 (attract): “The news of the magic brush drew the greedy Zamindar from his palace.” Each sentence must have “drew” (or “draw”) underlined and used in the correct sense.

items.item_stem:
Rewrite the three sentences below, inserting the most appropriate interjection from the box at the beginning of each sentence. Write the interjection followed by a comma, then the rest of the sentence.
[ Whoa / Ouch / Hey ]

1. ________, did you see Gopi paint that bowl of khichdi into existence?
2. ________, the Zamindar grabbed the magic brush and scratched his hand on a sharp edge.
3. ________, that fortress the Zamindar wants would take a hundred years to build!

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Hey, did you see Gopi paint that bowl of khichdi into existence?  2. Ouch, the Zamindar grabbed the magic brush and scratched his hand on a sharp edge.  3. Whoa, that fortress the Zamindar wants would take a hundred years to build!

items.item_stem:
Read the two riddles below and write the answer for each in one word or a short phrase.

Riddle 1: I have cities but no houses, I have forests but no trees, and I have rivers but no water. What am I?

Riddle 2: I am tall when I am young and short when I am old; in a dark room my story is told. What am I?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Riddle 1: A map.  Riddle 2: A candle.

items.source_lo: Student engages in lateral thinking and creative extension using hands-on exploration as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four riddles about seemingly unreal phenomena; design of an original magical object for a community purpose.
items.item_stem: In the poem, Gopi’s magic brush is powerful because it serves the community rather than one person. Design a new magical object of your own. In a short paragraph (80–100 words), describe: (a) what the object looks like, (b) its one special magical quality, and (c) how it would benefit a community or group of people in need. Give your object a name.

expected_elements: Names the object and gives a clear visual description.
Defines one specific magical quality (not vague or all-powerful).
Explains a community benefit, naming who it helps and how.
Writing is coherent, within the word range, and uses vivid detail.
